subject: Calibration of softmax outputs and how to measure expected calibration error

Topic: Calibration of softmax outputs and how to measure expected calibration error

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-18)
response:
Softmax outputs are probability-like numbers that sum to 1, but the central question of calibration is whether those numbers are accurate frequencies: if a model outputs 0.9 for a class, does it actually get that class right 90% of the time? Expected Calibration Error (ECE) answers this by bucketing predictions by confidence, measuring the gap between average confidence and actual accuracy in each bucket, and averaging those gaps weighted by bucket size. The key concepts are reliability diagrams (plots of confidence vs. accuracy that make miscalibration visible), temperature scaling (a post-hoc fix that sharpens or softens the distribution by dividing logits by a scalar), and the distinction between overconfidence (the common case in modern deep nets) and underconfidence.

What a beginner misses: ECE is acutely sensitive to binning choices — equal-width bins behave very differently from equal-mass bins, and with sparse or skewed data you can get wildly different ECE values from the same model just by changing bin count. Experts also worry that ECE is a marginal statistic: it averages over all inputs, so a model can have low ECE globally while being badly miscalibrated on a specific subpopulation (e.g., rare classes or distribution-shifted inputs). Finally, softmax overconfidence is structurally baked in — even a randomly initialized network tends to produce high-confidence outputs because the softmax exponential amplifies small logit differences, so good calibration requires deliberate intervention, not just good accuracy.

When you double the bins from 10 to 20, ECE typically increases because more bins means thinner bins means sparser bins — and sparse bins produce noisier accuracy estimates, so the confidence-accuracy gaps look larger on average. Naeini et al. (2015), who popularized ECE, used 10 bins somewhat arbitrarily, and subsequent work (notably Kumar et al., 2019, "Verified Uncertainty Calibration") showed empirically that ECE estimates on standard benchmarks like CIFAR-10 can shift by 1–3 percentage points just from rebinning, with no change to the model. This variance is not just numerical noise — it means two papers can report contradictory calibration rankings for the same pair of models depending on their binning choice, which has actually happened in the temperature scaling literature. The instability tells you ECE is measuring a sample statistic that approximates something real (the true integral of squared confidence-accuracy gap), but the approximation is poor in the tails where predictions cluster near 0 or 1 and bins become nearly empty. A more principled alternative is the kernel density ECE (Zhang et al., 2020) or the debiased ECE (Kumar et al., 2019), which replace hard bin boundaries with smooth estimates and have better statistical properties — at the cost of a hyperparameter (bandwidth) replacing the bin-count hyperparameter, which is a lateral move as much as a fix. The practical takeaway for an expert is: never report a single ECE number without also reporting bin count and bin scheme, and treat ECE differences smaller than ~1–2% as statistically meaningless on typical dataset sizes.

response:
Temperature scaling applies a single scalar T to all logits before softmax, which means it performs a global recalibration — it can shift the entire confidence distribution left or right, but it cannot fix miscalibration that varies across regions of input space or across classes. The structural limitation is that it preserves the rank ordering of confidences and the relative shape of the logit distribution — it stretches or compresses uniformly, so if the model is overconfident on easy inputs but underconfident on hard inputs (a pattern documented in Guo et al., 2017, "On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks"), a single T cannot simultaneously fix both. This bites hardest in class-imbalanced settings: the majority class typically gets high-confidence, well-separated logits while minority classes get low-confidence, compressed logits, and the optimal T for the majority class is different from the optimal T for the minority — but you can only pick one. It also fails badly under distribution shift: T is fit on a validation set drawn from the training distribution, and Ovadia et al. (2019, "Can You Trust Your Model's Uncertainty?") showed that calibration degrades sharply as covariate shift increases, with temperature-scaled models sometimes performing worse than uncalibrated baselines under strong shift because the fitted T is simply wrong for the new distribution. The fix requires either input-conditional calibration (e.g., local temperature scaling, where T is a function of the input) or class-wise temperature scaling (Kull et al., 2019, "Beyond temperature scaling"), both of which add parameters and require more validation data to fit without overfitting the calibration procedure itself.

The single most important diagnostic is stratified calibration by clinically meaningful subgroups — specifically, computing separate reliability diagrams and ECE scores for subpopulations defined by disease severity, demographic variables, or acquisition conditions (e.g., scanner manufacturer in radiology). The reason this dominates is that a medical model's aggregate ECE can look acceptable — say 2–3% — while being catastrophically miscalibrated on the subgroup that matters most clinically: the high-severity patients where the model's output will actually change a decision. This exact failure mode appeared with Google's diabetic retinopathy model (Gulshan et al., 2016, and subsequent deployment analyses): aggregate AUC and calibration metrics were strong, but performance degraded substantially on images from certain camera types and patient demographics underrepresented in training, something invisible in the top-line numbers. The stratification should be done along outcome-severity axes as well as demographic ones — for a cancer screening model, you want separate calibration curves for true positives at different Gleason scores or tumor stages, because underconfidence on high-grade disease is a categorically different failure from overconfidence on benign findings. Beyond ECE, within each stratum you want the reliability diagram rather than just a scalar, because a stratum with only 50 patients might have acceptable ECE by coincidence while showing a systematic monotonic miscalibration pattern (always under by ~10pp) that the scalar obscures. Ovadia et al. (2019) make the related point that uncertainty estimates from all methods they tested — including MC Dropout and deep ensembles — degraded under shift, and subgroup stratification is the closest proxy available pre-deployment for catching that degradation before it harms patients.

response:
The top-class framing collapses the entire output distribution into a single number — the confidence in the argmax prediction — and throws away all information about how probability mass is distributed across the remaining classes, which is precisely the information a clinician needs when the differential diagnosis is the output. If a dermatology model assigns 0.4 to melanoma, 0.35 to basal cell carcinoma, and 0.25 to seborrheic keratosis, top-class ECE treats this identically to a 0.4 / 0.01 / ... / 0.01 distribution, even though the first case should trigger a biopsy for two conditions and the second arguably for one — a clinically meaningful difference that calibration metrics completely ignore. The correct framing is classwise calibration: for each class k, treat the model's output p_k as a binary probability that "this case belongs to class k," build a separate reliability diagram, and compute a per-class ECE — this was formalized in Kull et al. (2019) and is sometimes called the marginal calibration condition. Beyond marginal calibration, the stricter requirement is joint or canonical calibration (Widmann et al., 2019, "Calibration tests in multi-class classification"), which asks whether the full predicted probability vector matches the true conditional class distribution — a condition that marginal calibration can satisfy while joint calibration fails, because each binary margin can be correct while the joint vector is systematically distorted. In practice, a reasonable measurement suite for a 10-class medical model is: per-class reliability diagrams (catches class-specific over/underconfidence), the classwise-ECE average, and a label-conditional calibration test that checks whether E[p_k | Y=k] ≈ accuracy within class k — the last one being particularly important for rare disease classes where marginal ECE is dominated by the common classes and minority-class miscalibration is invisible.

Consider a 3-class skin lesion model (melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, benign) that is classwise-calibrated: among all cases where p(melanoma)=0.6, roughly 60% are melanoma; among all cases where p(BCC)=0.6, roughly 60% are BCC. But suppose the model systematically outputs (0.6, 0.6, -0.2) — normalized to (0.46, 0.46, 0.08) — whenever the input is ambiguous between melanoma and BCC, even though the true distribution for those ambiguous cases is (0.5, 0.4, 0.1). Each marginal looks fine in isolation, but the joint vector is wrong: the model is systematically overconfident that ambiguous cases are one of the two malignant classes relative to the true joint, which means a decision rule that biopsies when max(p_melanoma, p_BCC) > 0.7 would trigger too often, increasing unnecessary procedures — the exact cost-calibration tradeoff that Lasko et al. and subsequent health ML work identify as a primary deployment failure mode. Fixing joint calibration requires learning a mapping from the full K-dimensional simplex to a corrected K-dimensional simplex, not K independent binary recalibrations — the standard tool is matrix scaling (a K×K matrix applied to logits, generalizing temperature scaling's scalar) or Dirichlet calibration (Kull et al., 2019), which fits a Dirichlet distribution over the simplex and has closed-form gradients. Dirichlet calibration requires estimating K² + K parameters, which means it needs substantially more validation data than temperature scaling — for a 10-class problem that's 110 parameters, and with typical medical validation sets of a few hundred cases per class you risk overfitting the calibration map itself. The deeper algorithmic constraint is that no post-hoc method can add information the model's logits don't contain — if the model's internal representation genuinely cannot distinguish the melanoma-vs-BCC ambiguous cases, no calibration map fixes the joint distribution; it can only redistribute existing probability mass, not create new discriminative signal.

The class of miscalibration that logit-only methods cannot fix is input-conditional miscalibration: systematic confidence errors that depend on where in input space the example lies, not just on the confidence value itself. A concrete instance — the model is well-calibrated on high-contrast, well-lit dermoscopy images but overconfident by ~15pp on low-quality or motion-blurred images; the logits for a blurry image and a sharp image can be identical in magnitude, so any function of logits alone assigns them the same calibrated confidence, even though their true accuracies differ. This is the failure mode documented in Nixon et al. (2019, "Measuring Calibration in Deep Learning") where they show residual miscalibration after temperature scaling correlates with input covariates like image brightness and contrast — the scalar T fixes the marginal but leaves input-conditional gaps intact. The minimal architecture change that addresses this is input-conditional temperature scaling: replace the scalar T with a small auxiliary network T(x) — typically 2–3 fully connected layers on top of a frozen penultimate-layer embedding — that predicts a sample-specific temperature from the input features, then divides the logits by T(x) before softmax. Ding et al. (2021, "Local Temperature Scaling") and Zhang et al. (2020) both demonstrate this approach, showing 20–40% reduction in ECE over global temperature scaling on corrupted image benchmarks, with the auxiliary network adding fewer than 100K parameters to a ResNet-50. The key implementation constraint is that T(x) must be trained on a held-out calibration set with a proper scoring rule loss (typically NLL), not on the training set, to avoid the auxiliary network simply learning to mimic the base model's confidence and collapsing back to a constant — which is the most common failure mode when practitioners implement this without careful data splitting.

The sharpest argument is that classification loss explicitly discards information irrelevant to the argmax decision boundary — two inputs that are confidently classified identically will have nearly identical penultimate embeddings regardless of how different their epistemic uncertainty is, because the loss never penalized that conflation. Concretely: a sharp, high-quality image of an unambiguous lesion and a blurry, low-quality image of the same lesion type may both produce logits like (4.2, 0.3, 0.1), land near the same point in embedding space, and thus receive the same T(x) — even though the blurry image warrants much higher uncertainty; the embedding simply never learned to separate "confident because clear" from "confident because overfit to noise." The empirical evidence that this matters comes from Minderer et al. (2021, "Revisiting the Calibration of Modern Neural Networks"), who showed that Vision Transformers are better calibrated than ResNets out of the box — and their analysis suggests this is partly because ViT embeddings preserve more input-variation structure due to the attention mechanism, implying that embedding geometry genuinely affects downstream calibration quality. More directly, Galil et al. (2023, "What Can We Learn from the Selective Prediction and Uncertainty Estimation Performance of 400+ ML Models?") found that calibration quality across architectures correlates with the intrinsic dimensionality of the penultimate embedding — models with higher-dimensional, less collapsed representations tend to be better calibrated post-hoc — which is exactly what you'd expect if the mismatch is fundamental. The practical implication is that fixing this properly requires either (a) training with an auxiliary calibration objective on the embedding (e.g., adding a contrastive loss that separates high- and low-uncertainty inputs in embedding space) or (b) using a separate encoder trained explicitly on uncertainty-relevant signals like image quality, acquisition metadata, or out-of-distribution scores — neither of which is standard practice, meaning most deployed input-conditional calibration methods are working around a structural deficit in their features.
